title: Transactions, concurrency, and architecture
summary: Explain atomic updates, concurrent access, transaction management, and the trade-offs of centralized, parallel, and distributed architectures.
objectives: Explain atomicity with a transfer example
Separate transaction management from concurrency control
Compare centralized, parallel, and distributed deployment models

sections.title: One logical function, one consistent outcome
sections.body: A transaction is a collection of operations that performs one logical function. A transfer should either complete as a whole or leave the database unchanged; partial writes create an inconsistent state.

sourceLens.whyExaminable: Atomicity and concurrency are the bridge from a schema/query answer to a safe multi-user system.

sections.title: Architecture changes the cost model
sections.body: Centralized, client-server, parallel, and distributed systems differ in where data and computation live and how nodes communicate. A shared-nothing design can scale, but network coordination and data movement become explicit costs.

sourceLens.whyExaminable: Architecture questions ask you to connect a logical operation to failure, coordination, and placement assumptions.

examples.title: Bank transfer as a transaction
steps: Read account A and subtract the amount.
Write the new value of A.
Read account B and add the amount.
Write the new value of B.
Commit only when the logical function is complete.
examples.answer: Transaction management protects the database from failure; concurrency control protects interactions among concurrent transactions.

contrastDrills.prompt: Which property says a transfer is all-or-nothing?
contrastDrills.explanation: Atomicity treats a transaction as one indivisible logical unit; concurrency control manages interactions among simultaneous transactions.
contrastDrills.misconception: Name the boundary between the two concepts before choosing.

contrastDrills.prompt: Which architecture explicitly includes geographical distribution or heterogeneous schemas?
contrastDrills.explanation: The lecture distinguishes distributed databases by geographical placement and possible schema/data heterogeneity.
contrastDrills.misconception: Name the boundary between the two concepts before choosing.

math.explanation: A transfer is one logical function even though it contains multiple reads and writes. Atomic transaction semantics prevent a failure between the updates from exposing only one side of the transfer.
math.name: Atomic transfer invariant
math.purpose: Use it to show why both account updates belong to one transaction.

criticalQuestions.prompt: Why does transaction scope follow the business function rather than one SQL statement?
criticalQuestions.angle: Find the failure point between two individually valid updates.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: The business invariant links both updates. A transaction groups them so the database cannot commit only one half after a crash or abort.

criticalQuestions.prompt: How is isolation different from atomicity in the transfer example?
criticalQuestions.angle: Separate an all-or-nothing outcome from the visibility of concurrent intermediate states.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: Atomicity prevents a partial transfer from committing; isolation controls whether another transaction can observe or interfere with intermediate work before the transfer commits.
